analysis.one_liner: Requires oil and gas drillers on federal and tribal lands to capture gas now vented or flared.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 65 House Democratic cosponsors and one subcommittee hearing, but never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have locked in Obama-era methane rules as law and required companies drilling on federal and tribal lands to stop wasting natural gas. Operators would have to capture 85% of the gas from each well within three years and 99% within five, ban routine venting and flaring of new wells, measure every cubic foot of gas lost, and publish that data free online. Companies that vented or flared gas without permission would owe penalties worth three times the gas's market value.
analysis.who_benefits: People living near oil and gas fields get cleaner air, since venting and flaring release methane alongside pollutants that aggravate asthma and other health problems. Taxpayers gain because gas from federal leases belongs partly to the public — gas that is vented or flared is gas that never gets sold and never pays royalties. Methane is a greenhouse gas far more potent than carbon dioxide over the near term, so everyone gains some protection against climate change.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People near wells, taxpayers, everyone breathing

how_it_helps.text: Writes the EPA's 2016 methane emission standards for new and modified oil and gas sources directly into law, so a future administration could not quietly repeal them by rulemaking.

Requires the Interior Department to issue rules cutting gas waste from venting, flaring, and leaks on federal and tribal lands, with operators capturing at least 85% of the gas from each onshore well within three years and 99% within five years.
Reinstates the November 2016 waste-prevention rule that had been rolled back, until the new rules take effect.
Requires every operator to measure and report all gas produced, consumed on site, or lost through venting, flaring, or leaks, and to make that data publicly available on the internet free of charge.

Imposes civil penalties for unauthorized venting and flaring equal to three times the market value of the gas, plus production restrictions, and requires all operators to run regular leak-detection inspections with prompt repairs.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies drilling on federal and tribal lands would bear the cost: replacing high-bleed pneumatic devices, installing meters on flared gas, running leak-detection programs, and building the capture infrastructure the mandates assume. Some of that cost would be passed to consumers through higher prices, and operators in basins without enough pipelines to carry captured gas would face the hardest choices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas operators on federal lands

drawbacks.text: The bill bans flaring for all new and refractured wells and requires near-total capture, but some drilling regions lack the pipelines and processing capacity to move captured gas to market; meeting the mandate there could mean slowing or halting production.
Compliance costs fall on operators of every size, since the requirements apply regardless of how small the operation is, and smaller operators have the least capacity to absorb them.
By codifying the 2016 EPA rule, the bill narrows the agency's flexibility: it may revise those standards only if the revision would reduce gas release.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefits — less methane pollution, cleaner air near wells, and royalties on gas that is currently burned off or leaked for free — are large and fall on everyone. The costs fall on a specific set of companies, and in basins without adequate pipeline capacity the 99% capture mandate would be genuinely difficult. The overall design is demanding but coherent; the heaviest burdens land where the infrastructure to comply may not yet exist.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in May 2019, the bill was sent to two House committees, got a single subcommittee hearing in September 2019, and then sat with no markup and no vote until the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Diana DeGette introduced the bill on May 14, 2019 with four original cosponsors, and it was referred to both the Natural Resources Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee.
Sixty-five House Democrats eventually cosponsored the bill; no House Republican did.
The bill was referred to subcommittees in both committees within three weeks of introduction.
The only substantive action after referral was a subcommittee hearing on September 24, 2019.
Neither committee ever reported the bill, and it never received a floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies operating on federal and tribal lands are better off, since they avoided capture mandates, metering requirements, and penalties worth three times the market value of gas they vent or flare. Taxpayers also lose the royalties they would have collected on gas that is currently wasted rather than sold.

sides.party_line_note: All 65 cosponsors, plus the sponsor, were House Democrats; no Republican signed on. With Democrats controlling the House, the bill's obstacle was committee inaction rather than a floor defeat.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers on federal and tribal lands
industries.note: The bill would have required these operators to capture 85% then 99% of the gas from each well, replace leak-prone equipment, install meters, and pay triple the market value of any gas they vented or flared without authorization. Today, gas they vent or flare is gas that pays no royalties to the public and adds methane to the air near nearby communities.

The bill mandates infrared leak-detection inspections, low-bleed or no-bleed pneumatic devices, meters on flared gas, and upgraded tanks, compressors, and pumps — a large market for detection and capture equipment. That interest runs alongside the public's, since the equipment is what makes the pollution cuts happen.
